units.quote:
Mangroves on dykes and in ponds often hamper pond maintenance, and their litter and 
shade reduce pond productivity. Leaves from these mangroves will decompose in the 
ponds. This decomposition may provide feed sources to the shrimp and other cultured 
organisms. But with too many mangroves, or when the pond water is not refreshed 
regularly, this litter increases ammonia levels in the water, decreases the dissolved 
oxygen content, and thus reduces pond productivity.

relationship.outcome_raw: pond productivity of silvo-aquaculture ponds with mangroves planted on dykes and in the pond (litter raises ammonia, lowers dissolved oxygen; shade)

context.practice_as_described: Classical silvo-aquaculture: mangroves planted on the pond dykes and in the pond. BASELINE = the same extensive pond without trees in or on it (implied; no measured comparison).
context.note: Technical guideline p7, practitioner assertion (no data); the same claim on p4 cites ref [18] ('may even have negative effects on aquaculture'). Applies to in-pond / on-dyke planting only - the guideline's alternative (AMA: mangrove greenbelt OUTSIDE the pond) is asserted to allow yields 'identical as for the normal intensive farms' (p5) but with no measurement and against an intensive-farm benchmark, so not emitted. Grey literature from the BwN / Wetlands International programme promoting AMA (COI cluster; positive-bias risk for AMA, but this unit is a negative for the competing design). Timescale assumed (trees large enough to shade/litter).

units.quote:
Generally, seedling survival was more sensitive to sediment
erosion than to accretion. For all species, signiﬁcantly more
seedlings died under erosion than accretion treatments (Fig. 3;
Supplementary Tables S2, S3). In fact, all species survived
accretion except the seedling of the small pioneer S. apetala
(2/12 died) that had grown signiﬁcantly shorter shoots than
the other species over the course of the 34-day experiment

context.note: Replicated mesocosm experiment (12 replicates per species x treatment; randomisation not stated -> quasi_experimental). Species result (kept per t3t6bl_G1). S. apetala is non-native in China (introduced from Bangladesh for afforestation, p2). Mechanism (p11): small propagules are buried most easily - 'to avoid the risks of complete burial, it is best to be tall'.

conditions expected annual damage (EAD) to built-up assets 
caused by overtopping of coastal defenses linked to storm 
surge and wave-related flooding could potentially be reduced 
by US$800 million per year, which is equivalent to 2.3% of 
total damage projected for mangrove coastlines (Fig.  1). In 
addition, the number of expected annual affected population 
(EAAP) by flood risk can be reduced by 140,000 (3%).

context.practice_as_described: MODELLED restoration of all potentially restorable mangrove areas (areas of recent 1996-2016 mangrove loss, Worthington & Spalding restoration-potential model) on the foreshore in front of dikes (hybrid 'vegetated foreshore + dike' coastal defence). BASELINE: the same dikes (FLOPROS protection standards) with present mangrove widths (Global Mangrove Watch 2010) and no restoration; benefit = difference between the two flood-risk runs (p2, p8).
context.note: Global model (PNAS 2026; restoration explicitly modelled): van Zelst XBeach wave-attenuation lookup + EuroTop dike overtopping on 495,361 shore-normal transects, GLOFRIS coastal flood risk at ~1 km, GTSR surge enriched with IBTrACS cyclones (p8). ONE DATASET, ONE UNIT (#61): the same runs give expected annual damage (EAD) to built-up assets reduced by US$800 million/yr = 2.3% of damage on mangrove coastlines (same quote); future 2080 reductions 3.8% (EAD) and 5.4% (EAAP) of total impacts (p2); West Africa has the largest relative reduction, 11% of EAD and 18% of EAAP, Southeast Asia the largest absolute (p2). People-affected chosen because T3 is risk to livelihoods. Strength slight (3% < 10% band) - the global share is diluted by coastlines with no restoration potential; residual risk 'remains high' (p2). Authors' caveats (p6-7): assumes functional dikes everywhere mangroves are restored (many restoration sites lack dikes, so benefit may be over- or under-stated); restored stands assumed to keep pace with sea level; cyclone damage to mangroves NOT modelled; wave attenuation nonlinear in forest width, so small patches add little. units.citation: (2022). The Economics of Large-scale Mangrove Conservation and Restoration in Indonesia. .
units.quote:
We estimated blue carbon sequestration by calculating how 
much mangrove restoration reduced CO2 concentrations in the 
atmosphere.  We used measurements reported in Cameron 
et al. (2019) of GHG emissions of t 17 ± 5.6 tCO2e per year 
from partially inundated aquaculture ponds in Indonesia with 
no mangrove coverage. Then, we added a 15 ± 5 tCO2e per 
year biomass sequestration rate from mangrove restoration 
(average 35 years) as estimated by Cameron et al. (2018). 
Finally, we added the soil carbon burial estimated in 6.5 ± 2.1 
tCO2e per year by Alongi (2014) to come up with a total blue 
carbon reduction per year per hectare of 38.5 ± 12.7 tCO2e.

relationship.outcome_raw: net GHG reduction per hectare per year from restoring mangrove on aquaculture ponds: avoided pond emissions + biomass sequestration + soil carbon burial

context.practice_as_described: Mangrove restoration (regrowth over an average 35 years) on former partially inundated aquaculture ponds. Baseline: pond with no mangrove cover, emitting GHG.
context.note: Annex A2, p39 (Table 3, p40). An accounting chain of three cited primaries, not a new measurement: pond baseline 17 ± 5.6 tCO2e/yr (Cameron et al. 2019), biomass 15 ± 5 tCO2e/yr (Cameron et al. 2018, median of fringing/estuarine mangroves), soil burial 6.5 ± 2.1 tCO2e/yr (Alongi 2014, average for ESTABLISHED forest). The avoided-emissions term (17) is a counterfactual baseline, so the 38.5 total is larger than the stand's own uptake (15 + 6.5). Conservation figure (271 tCO2e/ha avoided, 25% of 1,083 tCO2e stock) is an assumption for EXISTING mangrove and was not emitted.

units.citation: Takagi (2023). Survival of young planted mangroves in a calm bay environment during a tropical cyclone. Nature-Based Solutions.
units.quote:
Seven months after planting, one of the seven mangroves dis­
appeared for unknown reasons. Six plants survived for 31 months in 
good condition; however, after 36 months, withered leaves were 
observed in two of the mangroves. As shown in Fig. 4, Typhoon Haishen 
occurred 16 months after planting, indicating that the typhoon did not 
cause any external damage to the six mangroves.

relationship.outcome_raw: damage to young planted mangroves from a strong typhoon passing near the island 16 months after planting: none of the six surviving plants damaged

context.practice_as_described: PLANTING: seven Kandelia sp. propagules (average 19 cm) planted directly at the seaward (frontal) edge of an existing natural mangrove forest in the innermost part of a calm bay, May 2019; survival and growth monitored for 36 months (p9, p12). No unplanted comparison; the asset outcome is damage/loss of the planted stems during the event.
context.note: Results p9: 7 planted, 1 lost at 7 months for unknown reasons (before the typhoon), 6 survived 31 months; typhoon at 16 months caused no external damage; withered leaves on 2 plants at 36 months. Author caveats (abstract p2, conclusion p12-13): survival was partly FORTUITOUS - peak waves coincided with LOW TIDE and the site is deep inside a sheltered bay where offshore waves were strongly attenuated; modelled oscillatory acceleration of the young plants was ~1 g and would have been ~5 g at higher tide, enough to damage leaves. Author calls it 'a fairly strong typhoon' / 'one of the strongest typhoons of recent years' (p2, p4) - not mapped to a severity class (no inference). n = 6-7 plants, one site, one species: case-study weight. A one-metre Tonga tsunami (2022) also caused no visible damage, again at low tide (p12). Cited background (p3): Philippine plantings long-term survival 10-20% (Primavera & Esteban 2008) - not emitted (establishment survival, not hazard; cited secondary).
